# Detecting Human Trust Calibration in Automation: A Convolutional Neural Network Approach

Sanghyun Choo and Chang S. Nam

**Abstract—There is a general lack of studies that are aimed at monitoring and detecting an operator’s trust calibration, even though detecting someone’s adjusted trust towards automation is essential to prevent misuse and disuse of automation. The goal of this article is to propose a convolutional neural network (CNN) based framework to estimate operators’ trust levels and detect their trust calibration in automation using image features of electroencephalogram (EEG) signals preserving temporal, spectral, and spatial information. Thirteen participants performed a set of automated Air Force multiattribute task battery tasks that differed in reliability (High/Low) and credibility (High/Low) levels. The proposed framework was compared with three machine learning methods—naïve bayes, support vector machine, multilayer perceptron—in terms of accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of trust estimation and detection of trust calibration. Results of this article showed that the proposed framework had the highest performance of both trust estimation and detection of trust calibration in automation compared to the other comparison methods. This indicates that the proposed framework using the CNN classifier with the image-based EEG features could be an applicable model for estimating multilevel trust and detecting trust calibration during human-automation interaction. Also, it can help to prevent disuse and misuse of automation by estimating operators’ trust levels and monitoring their trust calibration in automation.**

**Index Terms—Convolutional neural network (CNN), deep learning (DL), electroencephalography (EEG), human-automation interaction (HAI), machine learning (ML), trust calibration, trust estimation.**

## I. INTRODUCTION

<sup>EOPLE</sup> tend to misuse or fail to use complex autonomous systems, although such automation offers potential benefits through assisting them in accomplishing their tasks [1]. The misuse or disuse in automation is related to people’s trust in automation. For example, people tend to use automated systems they trust and not use automation they do not trust. More importantly, cases of disuse and misuse often occur when an operator’s trust in automation is poorly calibrated [2]. Trust calibration is defined as the process by which automated system operators learn to adjust their trust towards automation based upon the actual system performance and capabilities [3]. Factors that affect trust calibration include reliability [4], credibility [5], automation errors [6], individual differences in the causal attribution of automation errors [7], and task difficulty [8].

However, few quantitative methods exist, which can detect the calibration of an operator’s trust in an automated system in near real-time at the neural level. First, studies have shown that an operator’s calibrated trust towards automation can be identified [4], [6]–[8], but the calibrated trust was determined only after the task is completed [4]. Second, several models to forecast human trust have been proposed, but these models used mainly discrete, self-reported behavioral measurements [9] or continuous cognitive signals [10]. Neural correlates of trust between humans [11] and between human and machine [12] have also been explored, but only a few studies have investigated neural correlates of trust calibration in automation, and even fewer have used electroencephalogram (EEG), which has better temporal resolutions than those of other neuroimaging methods such as functional magnetic resonance imaging or functional near infrared spectroscopy [13]. Third, deep learning (DL) has been widely used in many challenging applications due to its effectiveness. For instance, in comparison to traditional machine learning (ML), convolutional neural networks (CNN) have demonstrated promising outcomes in mental workload [14], motor imagery [15], driving safety [16], and emotion recognition [17]. But little attention has been paid to developing an EEG-based DL method that can detect an operator’s trust calibration with estimated trust.

Additionally, it is essential to track human trust in automation since we can prevent overtrust and undertrust toward automation, which can lead to accidents [18], [19] and task performance degradation [20] of human-automation interaction (HAI). Also, it facilitates identifying when human trust in automation has become excessively high or lowered and identifying the causes that affect such results. Therefore, developing intelligent systems that can estimate trust and detect trust calibration towards automation is crucial.

The main goal of this article is to develop a CNN-based framework for detecting human trust calibration in automation using image-based EEG features maintaining temporal, spectral, and spatial information. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is then validated by comparing its prediction error with that of the four contemporary ML models that have been widely used to detect an operator’s cognitive state, such as naïve bayes (NB), support vector machine (SVM), and multilayer perceptron (MLP) (for details, see Section III-J2). The following three reasons for developing the proposed detection framework for human trust calibration in automation using a CNN based on the proposed EEG features introduces significant novelty to this article. First, EEG signals provide multidimensional information (e.g., time, frequency, channels). Hence, it is necessary to consider only relevant information to classify cognitive states. The noise and artifacts found in EEG signals make manual feature extraction difficult. However, the proposed EEG features can include most EEG information when it comes to spectral and spatial features. Second, few studies used CNN with EEG for the estimation of human trust [21], although CNN has shown promise in the EEG domain. So, we explore CNN’s ability to estimate human trust in automation using EEG. Third, most of the previous studies focused on inferring the trust level itself. However, we need to monitor operators’ trust calibration in automation to pre-vent adverse situations (e.g., automation disuse or misuse). So, we propose a framework to detect one’s trust toward automation early. The main contributions of this article are as follows.

1) A detection framework of trust calibration in automation using a CNN with image-based EEG features is proposed.

2) The framework exploits multilevel trust estimation based on the CNN to detect trust calibration in automation.

3) The proposed EEG features as neurological data include spectral and spatial information of the EEG in terms of human trust in automation.

4) All results show the proposed framework is a suitable model to both estimate human trust levels and detect human trust calibration in automation.

## II. RELATED WORK

## A. Computational Models for Trust

Studies on computational models for trust have been developed based upon experience [22] and self-reported measurements of humans [9], [23], [24]. Xu and Dudek [22] developed a method for near real-time human trust inference in robots using a dynamic Bayesian network based on each user’s experiences with robots. Robot performance, human intervention, and trust reports from the past are included for the factors for the experiences. Lee and Moray [23] attempted to infer human trust in automation dynamically by using both a regression model and a transfer function with a time series analysis based upon a self-reported assessment of human trust. Jonker and Treur [9] developed a dynamic prediction model, which included trust evolution and trust update for software agents depending on experiences. Nam et al. [24] employed a Markov decision process, which is a kind of reinforcement learning, to predict human trust in automation based on the learned behaviors of the operators. Those studies may not be suitable to estimate one’s trust level in real-time, because they relied on only the behavioral data. Neurological signals can be utilized to resolve this issue. Studies showed that neurological signals could be applied to recognize cognitive states successfully (e.g., emotion recognition [25], motor imagery [26], mental workload [27]) in real-time. Also, studies showed that neurological data can be utilized for estimating human trust levels. For example, Riedl and Javor [10] showed that trust level is generated in oxytocin, which is provided by the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary, as well as related to several brain regions especially the basal ganglia, the frontal cortex, and the limbic system. Also, several EEG studies investigated neural correlates of human trust. Boudreau et al. [28] concluded that participants had different peak values of event-related potential (ERP) when they took part in a coin-toss experiment that measured trustworthiness. Long et al. [29] showed the feedback-related negativity and the P300 of ERP were related to distrust choice and trust choice, respectively, based on the modified coin-toss experiment. De Visser et al. [13] found that observational error positivity (oPe), a type of ERP in observation stimuli, was significantly correlated with the subjective trust measures. Wang et al. [30] identified that the frontal and the occipital regions were significantly correlated with human trust in autonomous system using EEG-based analysis that included the signal time-dependency, complexity, and power spectrum density. Those studies showed that EEG can be utilized for estimating human trust since they revealed several correlation results between EEG properties and human trust. But there is still a lack of studies that use EEGs for estimating human trust in automation specifically. We found only one study, which used EEG to estimate human trust levels in machines. Akash et al. [31] proposed a real-time classifier to estimate binary level of human trust (trust or distrust) in machines using EEG and galvanic skin response (GSR). They used a quadratic discriminant classifier with several features (For EEG: mean, variance, peak-to-peak value, mean frequency, root mean square, signal energy; For GSR: net phasic component, maximum value of phasic activity) for estimating human trust in machines.

However, the previous studies have several limitations. First, the studies that used behavioral data for trust level can predict diverse levels of trust, but they are difficult to use for trust estimation in real-time due to the absence of neurological data. Second, the study using psychophysiological signals can only estimate binary trust levels (trust or distrust). From this model, we cannot know to what degree people trust a system. Third, there is still a lack of studies on estimating human trust in automation especially using EEG signals. Fourth, most of the previous studies focused on estimating trust level itself. However, detecting changes of trust levels is needed for advanced applications (e.g., prevention of misuse and/or disuse of automation). To overcome these limitations, we propose a detection method of trust calibration in automation and estimation of trust levels in terms of multiclass using CNN with image-based EEG feature.

## B. Convolutional Neural Network

DL has been widely applied in a variety of areas such as manufacturing, finance, and healthcare. A CNN is a kind of

DL approach which usually employs image data as input and includes particular layers such as convolution layers, pooling layers, and fully connected layers for classification problems [32]. The convolution layer can extract a variety of feature maps that can reduce complexity of images due to weight sharing by the convolution operator [33]. The pooling layer reduces spatial resolution of the extracted feature maps by convolution. The main advantage of the pooling is that it can make strong feature maps by preventing shift and distortion. Usually, average or max pooling are used for the pooling layer. The fully connected layer is placed after all convolution and pooling layers to classify the dataset depending on class. This layer transforms two-dimensional (2-D) or 3-D image datasets into 1-D feature maps. After that, the 1-D feature maps are connected with a softmax operator for classification, which can represent the probability distribution of a list of potential classes.

A CNN has several main advantages. First, it can detect and extract important features without any human inspection. Second, it is more computationally efficient than existing neural networks like MLP. This is because it has special convolution and pooling layers that can reduce data complexity and data resolution effectively using parameter sharing. CNNs have been applied in various domains (e.g., speech detection [34], facial recognition [35], image classification [36]). It also has been applied to EEG with more promising results (e.g., mental workload [37], motor imagery [15], emotion recognition [38]) than, the existing ML techniques (e.g., SVM, NB, MLP), especially in terms of classification problems. Given the CNNs’ versatility in a variety of areas and its advantages, we used CNNs to estimate trust levels and detect trust calibration in our experiment.

## III. MATERIALS AND METHODS

## A. Participants

Thirteen participants (12 men; mean age = 25.0 years, SD = 3.8) were recruited from a local university. The recruited subjects’ gender and age on trust levels in automation were not considered since studies showed no age [39] and gender [40] differences in terms of human trust in automation. Participants were all right-handed as determined by the Edinburgh handedness inventory [41]. The consistent handedness is important because the brain lateralization is affected by handedness [42]. All participants had normal vision, no experience about the Air Force multiattribute task battery (AF-MATB), were free of neurological disorders, and were not taking any medication that affects the central nervous system. The article was approved by the institutional review board and written consent was provided by participants.

## B. Apparatus and Experimental Task

Our article utilized the system monitoring (SYSMON) subtasks of the AF-MATB, which is a computer-based multitasking environment simulating a flight to evaluate operator performance and mental workload [43]. In the SYSMON subtask, subjects monitored four dials that fluctuated up and down and whether the system identified automation failure well or not.

Fig. 1. (a) Task Environment of AF-MATB (from left to right, respectively; Automation Failure, Neutral, Automation Success). (b) Overall experimental procedure of this article.

The dials should be within a nominally acceptable range (e.g., two spaces up and down based on the long needle in the middle) to avoid adverse effects on the flight. In an automated mode of the SYSMON subtasks, the program is automated to detect and correct gage malfunctions (e.g., when the dials exceed the acceptable range). In the manual mode of the SYSMON subtasks for the active session, the participants were asked to press key buttons (e.g., F1–F4) if they observed an automation failure. Fig. 1(a) shows the environment of the tracking subtasks and situations (automation failure, neutral mode, and automation success).

## C. Experimental Design

The experiment was a 2 × 2 repeated-measures design with algorithm credibility and reliability. It was designed with two independent variables as within-subject factors: two reliability levels (Low, 60%; High, 80%) and two credibility levels (Novice = Low; Expert = High). Reliability of the system monitoring task was manipulated by increasing or decreasing the rate of the automation successes or failures. Credibility was manipulated by cover stories which the participants were required to read before the experiment began. These stories described the “expert” or “novice” teams, which developed the algorithms. In reality, there were no such algorithms, only the AF-MATB’s native scripting functions. To measure subjective trust, a questionnaire “To what extent do you trust the algorithm to accurately identify a gauge malfunction?” was used with a 0 (completely distrust) −9 (completely trust) Likert scale [44]. Subjects were asked to answer the question before the experiment (for block 0) and after each trial session (for block 1, 2, 3).

## D. Procedure

Participants had two training sessions to familiarize themselves with the SYSMON subtask before data collection began. As shown in Fig. 1(b), there were a total of three experimental blocks. Each block consisted of two active trials, in which subjects were asked to respond to automation failures with a button press, and four observational trials, during which subjects were asked to count the number of automation failures they observed. The observational sequence was counterbalanced between participants. Each trial session was two-minutes long, with 24 events distributed uniformly and randomly within each session. Participants were given 30-s breaks between trials and two-minutes breaks between blocks.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 2. Process of EEG feature extraction.

## E. Data Acquisition and Signal Processing

An EEG cap (Electro-Cap International, Inc.) with 62 active electrodes was used to collect EEG data, which were organized according to the modified 10–20 method [45] and covered the frontal, central, parietal, and occipital areas. The EEG signals were grounded between AFz and Fpz and referenced to the right ear lobe. A g.USBamp amplifier (g.tec Medical Engineering) was used to amplify the signal. The EEG sampling rate was 256 Hz. All EEG signals were bandpass filtered between 0 to 32 Hz, and notch-filtered at 60 Hz. This article used the automatic artifact removal algorithms for removal of ocular and muscular artifacts in the EEG signals [46]. The signals were epoched using event-locked time windows, ranging from 200 ms preceding automation failure of algorithm to 1000 ms following automation failure of algorithm. BCI2000 [47], MATLAB (The MathWorks), and EEGLAB [48] were used for EEG signal capture and preprocessing.

## F. Data Augmentation

To use DLs for classification, it is essential to have huge amounts of data for training the model. Collecting a lot of EEG signals during the experiment is difficult since that work is arduous and time-consuming [27]. Data augmentation methods can be a solution to supplement the amount of inadequate data. Also, it can help the DLs to improve their performance with the augmented dataset in terms of classification.

There are two common data augmentation methods used in EEG: sliding window and noise addition [27], [49]. The EEG signals consists of time series data, which are continuous in time domain. However, if the EEG signals are transformed by the sliding window, which rotates or shifts data, EEG information of the time domain will be lost, especially in the case of converting the signals to images [17]. To solve this issue, adding random noise to the EEG signals can be used since EEG signals include nonstationarity and randomness [17]. In this article, we added only Gaussian noise N(0, 0.2 uV) with 30 augmented multiple that had highest performance in EEG classification with its image feature validated by [17].

## G. Feature Extraction

The proposed feature extraction was based on two findings from [13]. First, observational error-related negativity and oPe, which are types of ERPs, were evoked when people observed automation failure. Second, the oPe was significantly correlated with subjective trust measures. As shown in Fig. 2 (feature extraction part), the EEG feature extraction consists of three steps. First, the event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) map with frequency bands (0–32 Hz) was extracted by the time-frequency decomposition based on a Morlet wavelet transformation. The reason why we used the ERSP is that it already showed its utility in an EEG feature and EEG classification problem [27]. Second, the ERSP was segmented into specific frequency bands, namely delta (δ; 0–4 Hz), theta (θ; 4–8 Hz), alpha (α; 8–16 Hz), and beta (β; 16–32 Hz), in our region of interest (ROI) with each EEG channel. We included the four frequency bands since the previous studies showed a strong relationship between the bands and human trust in automation [17], [50]. On the other hand, we excluded higher frequency bands than beta (e.g., gamma) since these bands reflect other neural processes (e.g., eye-movement and microsaccades) rather than cognitive processing [51]. The ROI of this study was between 150 ms and 210 ms after stimulus of last automation failure in each condition. The reason why the ROI was selected is that oPe was significantly correlated with the subjective measure of trust between 150 ms and 210 ms after detecting automation failure in the experimental domain [13]. After being segmented, the ERSPs of the four frequency bands in terms of each EEG channel were imaged as 10 x 10, respectively. The produced segmented images were combined into one image by arranging each frequency image in the horizontal and stacking these images according to each channel in the vertical direction. The processed feature image included temporal-spectral-spatial information of EEG in the ROI and had an image size of 40 x 620 (4 frequency bands x 62 EEG channels). Finally, we derived reduced and grayscaled EEG image data (28 x 28) from the combined image.

## H. Classifier and Estimation of Trust Level

1) Convolutional Neural Network: As shown in Fig. 2 (classification part), our proposed CNN structure includes five layers:

the input layer, convolution layer, max-pooling layer, fullyconnected layer, and output layer (for the CNN’s general structure, see [34]). $\mathrm { ~ A ~ } 9   \times   9$ convolution filter with stride 1 was employed in the convolution layer. $\mathrm { ~ A ~ } 2 \times 2$ max pooling filter with stride 2 was employed in the pooling layer. The used node number and the activation functions are represented in the Fig. 2. Also, batch normalization and the Adam optimizer [52] with default settings were used when training the model.

2) How to Estimate Trust Levels by EEG Features: The goal of this stage is to estimate trust levels of the subjects using classifiers based on supervised learning methods. The subjective trust values can be considered as categorical data since they have discrete integer values from 0 to 9. Therefore, the problem of estimation of trust level can be transformed into a classification problem using classes 0 through 9 (a total of 10 classes). With the transformed problem, there were two steps for the estimation processes of the trust values. First, the extracted EEG features were used for training classifiers with its fitted labels (0 to 9). Second, estimated trust levels were derived by the trained classifiers with their own features of the EEG signals.

## I. Detection of Trust Calibration

The proposed detection method of trust calibration aims at determining whether the input EEG signals are calibrated or not depending on conditions $( R _ { L } C _ { H } , \thinspace R _ { H } C _ { H } , \thinspace R _ { H } C _ { L } , \thinspace R _ { L } C _ { L } ; \thinspace R$ Reliability, C: Credibility, H: high, L : low). The detection of trust calibration was based on the estimated trust levels by the classifiers. The detection criteria for trust calibration are as follows.

The trust level $X ^ { ( n , q ) }$ , which is by subject n $\mathrm { ( n = 1 , 2 , } . . . , \mathrm { N } ;$ $\mathrm { N } = 1 3 )$ , measurement type q $( \mathsf { q } = 1 , 2 , . . . , \mathsf { Q } ;$ 1: true value, 2: estimate dvalue), condition type $\mathrm { ~ i ~ } ( \mathrm { i ~ } = 1 ,   2 , . . . ,   \mathrm { I } ;   1 : R _ { L } C _ { H }$ 2: $R _ { H } C _ { H } , 3 : R _ { H } C _ { L } , 4 : R _ { L } C _ { L } )$ and block j $\mathrm { ~ j ~ } ( \mathrm { j } = 1 , 2 , . . . , \mathrm { J } ; 1 ; 0$ block, 2: 1 block, 3: 2 block, 4: 3 block), forms the following matrix:

$$
\boldsymbol {X} ^ {(\boldsymbol {n}, \boldsymbol {q})} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c c c} x _ {1, 1} ^ {(n, q)} & x _ {1, 2} ^ {(n, q)} & \dots & x _ {1, J} ^ {(n, q)} \\ x _ {2, 1} ^ {(n, q)} & x _ {2, 2} ^ {(n, q)} & \dots & x _ {2, J} ^ {(n, q)} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ x _ {I, 1} ^ {(n, q, l)} & x _ {I, 2} ^ {(n, q)} & \dots & x _ {I, J} ^ {(n, q)} \end{array} \right]\tag{1}
$$

where $x _ { I , J } ^ { ( n , q ) }$ is the element of trust level $X ^ { ( n , q ) }$

The direction of trust calibration, which is denoted as $\begin{aligned} { \mathbf { \mathit { d } } ^ { ( n , q ) } = ( d _ { 1 } ^ { ( n , q ) } , \; d _ { 2 } ^ { ( n , q ) } , \; d _ { 3 } ^ { ( n , q ) } , \ldots , \; \widehat { d } _ { I } ^ { ( n , q ) } ) ^ { T } } \\ \end{aligned}$ , is defined as follows:

$$
d _ {i} ^ {(n, q)} = \left\{ \begin{array}{c} + 1, x _ {i, 1} ^ {(n, q)} <   x _ {i, 2} ^ {(n, q)} \\ - 1, x _ {i, 1} ^ {(n, q)} > x _ {i, 2} ^ {(n, q)} \\ 0, x _ {i, 1} ^ {(n, q)} = x _ {i, 2} ^ {(n, q)} \end{array} \right.\tag{2}
$$

where $x _ { i , l } ^ { ( n , q ) }$ is the trust level of ith condition, block 0 or block 1. $\text{" +1 " , " -1 " }$ , and $\text{" }0 \text{" }$ represent positive trust calibration, negative trust calibration, and trust maintenance, respectively.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 3. Proposed framework procedure to detect trust calibration.

The detection of trust calibration, which is denoted as $\boldsymbol { y } ^ { ( n ) } =$ $( y _ { 1 } ^ { ( n ) } , \; y _ { 2 } ^ { ( n ) } , \; y _ { 3 } ^ { ( n ) } , \ldots , \; y _ { I } ^ { ( n ) } ) ^ { T }$ , is as follows:

$$
y _ {i} ^ {(n)} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 1, d _ {i} ^ {(n, 1)} = d _ {i} ^ {(n, 2)} \& x _ {i, 2} ^ {(n, 1)} = x _ {i, 2} ^ {(n, 2)} \\ 0, \text {Otherwise} \end{array} \right.\tag{3}
$$

Based on (3), trust calibration can be detected accurately by considering the true trust value. Fig. 3 shows the summary of the proposed detection framework of trust calibration.

## J. Evaluation

1) Evaluation Parameters: To evaluate the proposed framework for trust estimation and detection of trust calibration, the following indices were used.

Accuracy (Acc.): Accuracy is the ratio of the correctly classified results to the whole classified results. It shows how good the test is at classifying both a true positive class and a true negative class. Mathematically, this can be stated as

$$
A c c. = \frac {\mathrm{TP} + \mathrm{TN}}{\mathrm{TP} + \mathrm{TN} + \mathrm{FP} + \mathrm{FN}}.\tag{4}
$$

Sensitivity (Sens.): Sensitivity is the ratio of the correctly classified positive classes to all positive assessment. It shows how good the test is at detecting a true positive class. The formula is as follows:

$$
S e n s. = \frac {\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP} + \mathrm{FN}}.\tag{5}
$$

Specificity (Spec.): Specificity is the ratio of the correctly classified negative classes to all negative assessment. It shows how good the test is at identifying a true negative class. Mathematically, this can be represented as

$$
S p e c. = \frac {\mathrm{TN}}{\mathrm{TN} + \mathrm{FP}}\tag{6}
$$

where true positive (TP): the number of samples classified in the positive class correctly; true negative (TN): the number of samples classified in the negative class correctly; false positive (FP): the number of samples classified in the positive class incorrectly; false negative (FN): the number of samples classified in the negative class incorrectly.

The three indices have been used to validate classification performances of models using EEG data as an input because they show the ratio of the correctly classified values to all the assessment types [27], [53]–[56]. High values represent the high performance of a classification model. With those reasons, we adopted the three indices for evaluating the proposed framework.

2) Comparison Classifiers Setting: To assess the effectiveness of the CNN-based detection method of trust calibration in automation, several ML models (NB, SVM, and MLP) were used to compare their performance regarding the estimation of trust level and the detection of trust calibration. The NB classifier is a probabilistic supervised learning model in which Bayes’ theorem is applied with naïve independence assumptions. This classifier assumes all features are unrelated given the class information. To be used for the classification model and parameter estimation, it uses maximum likelihood estimation. Also, it is a flexible classifier and used in EEG domains like motor imagery (MI) and emotion recognition [57] since it can handle any number of classes quickly in the environment of EEG data [58]. The SVM is a supervised learning method generally used for classification and regression [59]–[61]. The target of this method is to find a hyperplane, which can maximize margins between the feature space from the dataset by solving the dual problem of the primal optimization [59]–[61]. SVMs have been broadly applied in EEG data due to their powerful classification accuracy [62]. They have been used in various domains for the classification of EEG data (e.g., diagnosis of epilepsy [63] and emotion recognition [64]). The artificial neural network (ANN) is a learning system that mimics the biological neural networks of the brain [65] and also serves as the beginning of the DL classifier. This model is composed of numerous interconnected neurons [66] and is trained using a backpropagation algorithm [67]. Generally, ANN means MLP, which includes hidden layers to overcome the limitation of single-layer perceptron (XOR problem [68]). This model includes an input layer, hidden layer, and output layer including biases, and an activation function to handle the dataset. This method has been successfully applied to EEG signals by way of motor imagery [69] and mental workload [70]. The parameters of the comparison models are as follows: The NB was trained and used with a prior empirical distribution of the ERSP image data. For the SVM, the linear kernel function was used. In the case of MLP, two types were used (one hidden layer and three hidden layers). The MLP with one hidden layer had 50 hidden nodes and a sigmoid function. Its number of iterations and learning rate value were 100 and 0.05, respectively. The MLP with three hidden layers had 20 hidden nodes each including a ReLU function. It had an epoch number of 100 and a learning rate of 0.005.

3) Cross Validation: Given the evaluation parameters and the comparison models, ten-fold cross-validation with offline analysis was performed in this article to evaluate performance of trust estimation and calibration detection by the proposed method. The overall EEG features with subjective labels were separated initially into ten folders, and then eight folders (80%) were selected for the classifiers training, one folder (10%) was used for the validation and the remaining one folder (10%) was employed for the testing. Data augmentation was applied only in training dataset. These procedures were repeated ten times until every folder was used for the training.

The source code will be made available upon request to the corresponding author.

## IV. RESULTS

The results of the detection framework of trust calibration are comprised of three parts. First, the subjective measurements of trust and a trust calibration area are presented to give an understanding of trust calibration in automation and to show statistical analysis results of subjective trust ratings depending on the conditions. Second, the proposed CNN-based classifier is compared with the other classifiers in the domain of trust estimation. Third, in the perspective of the detection of trust calibration, the CNN is compared with the classifiers. The purpose of these two comparisons is to prove the effectiveness of the CNN and the validation of the proposed model in the domain of trust calibration detection.

## A. Subjective Trust Measure and Trust Calibration

The 2 (reliability: High, Low) x 2 (credibility: High, Low) x 4 (blocks: 0, 1, 2, 3) repeated measures ANOVAs for subjective trust levels were conducted based on the three self-reported trust measures; reliability, credibility, and time blocks. The results showed significant main effects of reliability $[ F _ { } ( 1 ,   1 2 ) = 9 . 2 8 ,$ $p < 0 . 0 1 , \eta _ { p } ^ { 2 } = 0 . 7 7 ]$ and credibility $F ( 1 , 1 2 ) = 5 . 5 1 , p < 0 . 0 5$ $\eta _ { p } ^ { 2 }   =   0 . 4 6 ]$ . Significant interaction effect of reliability x time block $[ F ( 3 , 3 6 ) = 9 . 9 0 , p < 0 . 0 0 0 1 , \eta _ { p } ^ { 2 } = 0 . 8 3 ]$ and credibility x time block $[ F ( 3 , 3 6 ) = 8 . 9 2 , p < 0 . 0 \dot { 0 } 0 1 , \eta _ { p } ^ { 2 } = 0 . 7 4 ]$ were also found.

A post hoc Tukey test showed that trust ratings of the high credibility were significantly higher only in time block 0 $( p   <   0 . 0 0 0 1 )$ . This result indicates that cover stories successfully established the subjects’ trust in the algorithms. The post hoc test revealed trust ratings of high reliability in time block 1 and 3 were significantly higher $( p < 0 . 0 1 )$ . This implies trust of subjects is changed only by actual automation performance (reliability) when they interact with the automation. Post hoc analyses showed a significant interaction in trust ratings between the low reliability and high credibility levels $(p < 0.0001);$ ratings in time block 0 were significantly higher than those in time block 1. Also, the post hoc tests showed trust ratings for the interaction of high reliability and low credibility in time block 0 were significantly lower $( p < 0 . 0 5 )$ than those in time block 1. Those two results imply that trust calibration occurred when the actual automation performance was decreased or increased regardless of credibility levels.

As shown in Fig. 4 and Table I, the average trust levels of all subjects and the standard deviation of the trust values are shown for each block and condition. In this figure and table, block 0 represents initial trust level toward the automation that was measured before the experiment. Besides block 0, three other blocks represent experimental blocks that were performed in the trust calibration experiment. Given the reported trust ratings (see Fig. 4 and Table I), condition 1 $( R _ { L } C _ { H } )$ and condition $3 ~ ( R _ { H } C _ { L } )$ were detected as trust calibration since their trust levels were changed while crossing over. Additionally, the initial trust level of the subjects was higher in $C _ { H }$ (condition 1 and 2)

This shows that the initial trust level of human in automation can be manipulated by reliability level and shows that our experimental task with the conditions can induce trust calibration.

## B. Comparison With Classifiers in Trust Estimation

Before applying the classifier to the detection stage of trust calibration, it is necessary to confirm each classifier’s performance in terms of the estimation of trust level. Table II shows the comparisons of the classifiers (NB, SVM, MLP – one hidden layer, MLP – three hidden layers, CNN) in terms of accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity for the performance of the trust estimation. All values were computed as the average values in terms of cross-validation (tenfold). As shown in Table II, the CNN had statistically higher performances than other comparison models for all evaluation parameters.

## C. Comparison With Classifiers in Detection of Trust Calibration

To validate the CNN-based detection framework for trust calibration, we compared the performance of each classifier in terms of the average accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity based on cross-validation results depending on condition types, as shown in Fig. 5. In all conditions, the CNN-based detection model had statistically higher values in terms of the average accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity than other four supervised learning models.

## V. DISCUSSION

The objective of this article was to propose a new framework for the detection of human trust calibration in automation using ERSP image-based CNN. From the subjective measurements, the average trust levels of the subjects were calibrated from Block 0 to Block 1 clearly in the cases of $R _ { L } C _ { H }$ and $R _ { H } C _ { L }$ Within the goal of this article, we derived a method of extracting features that preserve temporal-spectral-spatial information of EEG in order to estimate trust levels and detect trust calibration in automation. In this article, we found that the average accuracy of the trust estimation derived from CNN was 94.3% based on the extracted EEG feature, which is higher than other comparison classifiers. Also, it was confirmed that the CNN classifier had higher performance in terms of the mean accuracy of the detection of trust adjustment toward automation at all conditions $( R _ { L } C _ { H } { : } 9 4 . 2 \% , R _ { H } C _ { H } { : } 9 3 . 8 \% , R _ { H } C _ { L } { : } 9 4 . 0 \% , R _ { L } C _ { L } { : } 9 2 . 9 \% )$ than other compared classifiers. Given those results, the CNN classifier with the proposed EEG feature is the most suitable classification model among the selected models to estimate the trust levels and detect the trust calibration in automation. To our knowledge, our study is the first to propose the detection framework of trust calibration in automation using CNN based on EEG data.

## A. Computational Models for Human Trust

We validated the effectiveness of the proposed computational model for multiclass human trust using a CNN model and EEG data. According to Akash et al. [31], trust estimation based on experience [22] or self-reported ratings [9], [23], [24] without any psychophysiological signals have limitations, which prevent them from inferring human trust in real time. This is because we cannot measure our experience and self-reported trust levels as real-time. Akash et al. [31] showed their proposed trust estimation model using EEG and GSR data with self-reported trust measures can sense human trust in near real-time. So, it is necessary to use psychophysiological signals for real-time human trust measures. However, it is only in near real-time not complete real-time. Most studies, which use supervised learning to estimate trust level, require true output values like self-reported measures. They have a limitation in the real time domain since they do not know actual subjective trust levels in the period during which the measures are not surveyed. For this issue, semisupervised learning, which is a mixed version of supervised learning and unsupervised learning, might be one solution. The semisupervised learning can label unlabeled data using the labelled dataset. If we use this approach, we can label the psychophysiological signals not including the subjective trust measures.

## B. EEG Features for Human Trust

We applied ERSP, a practical EEG feature for mental workload classification [27], and time range based on the previous research [13] to extract compound EEG features, including temporal, spectral, and spatial information of EEG. We reconstructed the ERSP features with the time range by segmenting and combing them based on the frequency bands and channel information. The performances of the classifiers with the features showed that this feature could be a good candidate for estimating human trust and detecting trust calibration in automation due to their high classification performances. This represents that the proposed EEG features can contain neural patterns related to human cognition of trust in automation. Therefore, the ERSP-based EEG feature can be used to estimate human trust in automation as well as mental workload.

## C. Comparisons of Classification Performance Between CNN and Typical ML Techniques

The CNN had higher classification performance in both trust estimation and detection of trust calibration than other conventional ML techniques. The high performance of CNN has been confirmed in a variety of applications (e.g., sentiment classification [71], and detection of sociomoral reasoning level [72]) as compared to the traditional ML. Also, studies showed CNNs had higher performance in terms of EEG-based cognitive states recognition when compared to the traditional ML methods (e.g., SVM and MLP) [16]. Like the previous studies, CNNs had higher classification accuracy in terms of trust estimation and detection of trust calibration in our study. This is because CNNs have special layers (convolution layer and pooling layer)

that can extract features by reducing complexity and keeping important parts in the images automatically [34]. Also, EEG data augmentation might lead to the high performance of the CNN classifier by avoiding the curse of dimension. According to Fawzi et al. [73], data augmentation can improve the accuracy and robustness of classifiers by replicating and transforming the training dataset.

## D. EEG Data Augmentation

We applied Gaussian noise addition as EEG data augmentation method to mitigate the overfitting problem for the classifiers. We might get high classification performance of the CNN classifier since data augmentation can improve the performance and robustness of classifiers by regularizing the classifier [73]. Although the CNN classifier showed a high classification performance using the data augmentation method, the Gaussian noise addition can generate synthetic EEG signals that might be similar to the existing samples or beyond the properties of the EEG signals. This is because the Gaussian noise addition does not consider any distribution or information of the existing EEG signals. To overcome this issue, generative model-based data augmentation methods (e.g., generative adversarial network [74] and variational autoencoder [75] might be applied. These methods can reflect the distribution of the training samples to generate the artificial samples that are diverse but reflect the distribution of the original samples. Several studies showed that generative model-based EEG data augmentation can significantly improve classifiers’ performance for cognitive states recognition [76], [77]. Therefore, the performance of our classifier might be further improved by applying these methods.

## VI. CONCLUSION

While detecting an operator’s adjusted trust towards automation is important when assisting one’s performance in automated tasks, little attention has been paid to neurophysiological quantitative methods for monitoring trust calibration and pre-dicting trust level. This article validated the effectiveness of a CNN-based DL framework to estimate an operator’s trust level and detect their calibrated trust of automation using EEG-based ERSP feature, which preserves temporal-spectral-spatial information. The main contributions of this article are as follows. First, the framework can extract EEG features while retaining temporal-spectral-spatial information, which can help to train the classification model. Second, it produced a higher accuracy of the estimation of multilevel trust and the detection of trust calibration than the other classifiers (NB, SVM, MLP). Therefore, the proposed framework based on the CNN model using image-based EEG features can be a suitable model for estimating multiclass trust levels and detecting trust calibration. Third, to the best of our knowledge, the proposed model is the first study to provide a detector for human trust calibration in automation based on EEG. It can detect trust calibration and estimate the trust level in advance. Doing so would help avoid overtrust or undertrust toward automation by intervening and redesigning the automation system before the operators have such trust levels in automation. In conclusion, it would help to improve task performance and prevent adverse accidents in HAI.

Future work may address the limitations in this article. First, the sample size (n = 13) in this article might be a limitation, but our effect sizes were large. Despite alleviating concerns of low power by the effect sizes, further larger-scale studies are required in the future. Second, more varied classifiers should be explored in the future to compare this CNN, which had the highest performance out of the classifiers, with the different types of CNNs. Finally, different methods for data augmentation and the amount of augmented data need to be explored, although the noise addition method for the augmentation proved enough to train classifiers.
